Female Green frogs (Lithobates clamitans) attain a maximum snout–vent length of 10.5 cm [Li = 10.5 cm], a size that corresponds to substantial reproductive potential in this semi-aquatic ranid. At the culmination of the larval stage, metamorphosis occurs when tadpoles reach a body length of 3.00 cm , a developmental milestone marking the transition to a terrestrial juvenile existence. During the initial phase of life, the freshly deposited eggs, characterized by a diameter of 1.5 mm, yield recently emerged hatchlings with an exceedingly low wet weight of 0.0018 g [Wwb = 0.0018 g]. This minimal birth mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the yolk-dependent embryo, which relies entirely on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The capacity for rapid early growth, fueled by abundant aquatic prey, allows these larvae to navigate the perils of predation and pond desiccation before completing metamorphosis.

A reliable estimate for the age at birth, defined as the interval from oviposition to eclosion, is 5 days [ab = 5 days] when eggs are incubated at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This rapid hatching period, typical of many north-temperate ranids, minimizes the exposure of the vulnerable, jelly-coated eggs to aquatic predators and fungal pathogens. After the chorion ruptures, the newly emerged tadpoles, still possessing a visible yolk sac, begin a phase of endotrophic development before commencing active filter feeding on algae. The subsequent larval period is characterized by a steady increase in body dimensions, culminating in the metamorphic climax when the gill-breathing larva undergoes a dramatic body plan reorganisation. The timing of this transformation is highly sensitive to thermal conditions and resource availability, which can either accelerate or delay the development of limb buds and the resorption of the tail.

Sexual maturation in female Green frogs is initiated when individuals attain a snout–vent length of 3.26 cm [Lp = 3.26 cm], a size threshold that signals the onset of gonadal maturation and gametogenesis. Achieving this body length typically requires one or two growing seasons following metamorphosis, depending on local environmental productivity and thermal regimes. Upon reaching this size, juveniles transition from a purely somatic growth phase to one involving the allocation of resources toward the development of ovarian follicles. The ultimate body size for females, capped at a maximum snout–vent length of 10.5 cm, is considerably larger than that of most males, a pattern consistent with fecundity selection in this species. This sexual size dimorphism is linked to the premium placed on abdominal volume for egg production, as larger females can produce larger clutches and thus achieve higher reproductive success over their lifetimes.

The maximum reproductive rate, observed during optimal breeding conditions, reaches 19.2 eggs per day [Ri = 19.2 eggs per day] when water temperatures hover near 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This impressive daily output is sustained over a relatively constrained breeding season, during which gravid females deposit multiple gelatinous egg masses in shallow, vegetated littoral zones. The total annual reproductive output is the product of this daily fecundity and the duration of the breeding period, which typically spans several weeks in late spring and early summer. Under favorable conditions, a single female may contribute substantially to the larval cohort of a given pond, a strategy that compensates for high rates of egg and tadpole mortality. The ecological context of this reproductive effort—such as the density of conspecifics and the abundance of predators—strongly influences the realized fecundity in any given year.

The maximum recorded lifespan in the wild for the Green frog is 10 years [am = 10 years] when averaged over a mean annual temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], a longevity that places it among the longer-lived temperate ranids. This extended lifespan allows for repeated reproductive attempts across multiple years, offsetting the stochastic risks of juvenile mortality. The ultimate wet weight for females, based on the allometric scaling of body dimensions, reaches 128 g [Wwi = 128 g], a mass that reflects the accumulation of somatic tissues and reproductive reserves over several growing seasons. The contrast between the negligible 0.0018 grams at hatching and the 128 grams at senescence underscores the dramatic ontogenetic shift in biomass from a lecithotrophic larva to a reproductively active adult. This remarkable growth trajectory is sustained by a diet that transitions from filter-feeding on algae to active predation on invertebrates, a trophic switch that fuels the energetic demands of maturation and reproduction.
